title: Technology in Education: A Breaking Point, not a Turning Point
author: Caitlin Lucas
summary: A kindergarten teacher and mother argues that one-to-one devices, adopted as a pandemic stopgap, have quietly become the default way of delivering instruction in the youngest grades. She describes students whose weekend plans are all screens and who show withdrawal-like behaviours in the first days of school, taking three months to wean from independent device use. She questions whether data justify typing assignments in third grade or Google Slides projects in fifth, citing research linking handwriting to retention. She also criticises the flood of AI lesson-planning ads and districts encouraging teachers to outsource their thinking. Her proposal is that personal technology should wait until about fifth grade. The piece is first-person testimony rather than a data review.
points: Standardized testing moving online locks districts into one-to-one device models even for the earliest grades.
The teacher spends about three months weaning kindergartners off independent technology and rebuilding play and tactile skills.
Devices bought as learning tools are said to have become pacifiers and distractions, with time lost to logins and platforms.
A fifth grader spent more time choosing slide themes than understanding content, illustrating tech substituting for thinking.
AI ads aimed at teachers raise the question of how professionals outsourcing thinking can model pencil-and-paper work.
quotes: Now, I spend a majority of those first few days managing behaviors that look a lot like withdrawal—anger, irritability, difficulty concentrating, restlessness, etc.
I spend a solid three months, yes months, weaning students away from independent technology use in the classroom. After this time, I see their social confidence take flight.
This decision is handcuffing district administrators and school boards to one-to-one models for even the earliest grade levels, even if they aren’t taking tests.
What was purchased by districts as a learning tool is rapidly turning into a pacifier for students, a crutch, and yet another distraction.
I know that technology has a place for students. I just do not see how or why it should be introduced before fifth grade.
She had spent more time choosing a background theme than understanding the content.
If we, the professionals, are outsourcing our thinking, how are we supposed to encourage students that a pencil, paper, and their brain are more than sufficient for the six hours a day they are here?
